newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greek, Turkish row threatens WEU missions.
newsitem.headline: Greek, Turkish row threatens WEU missions.

text.p: Greek and Turkish rivalry spilled over into the Western European Union (WEU) on Tuesday, threatening to disrupt the European defence group's plans for peacekeeping and humanitarian aid efforts.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller warned that Ankara would block the use of NATO equipment by the WEU because of Greek objections to giving Ankara a strong say in WEU mission planning.
"Turkey will block all the support of NATO," Ciller was quoted as telling Turkish reporters at a news conference on the margins of a WEU ministerial meeting in the Belgian seaside town of Ostend.
"The WEU can do nothing without the support of NATO," she said.
Reporters said Ciller was furious about Greece's actions at the WEU meeting. She left the meeting hurriedly after the news conference.
The WEU, the European Union's fledgling defence arm, plans to conduct peacekeeping and humanitarian aid missions using equipment lent by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
NATO, with the blessing of the United States, agreed to lend its materiel to the WEU when Europeans wanted to act alone, particularly without the United States.

Greece said it had refused to accept a plan by the 10- member WEU to give associate members -- Norway, Iceland and Turkey -- an effective veto over future WEU operations by making decisions to undertake them based on consensus.
All three associate members are full members of NATO and could, if they wished, block the WEU from having any alliance equipment.
Ciller said it was time Greece, a longtime rival, viewed issues in a global manner, Turkish reporters said.

George Papandreou, Greece's European affairs minister, told Reuters that Athens had no problem with Turkey participating in WEU activities, but that it believed an associate member should not be given an effective veto.
"It was not in any way to say that Turkey cannot be involved," he said.
The two countries, despite being NATO allies, almost came to war earlier this year over uninhabited islets in the Aegean. The United States stepped in to broker a deal easing the tension.
WEU Secretary General Jose Cutileiro said he hoped the Belgian predidency of the WEU could sort the issue out before the end of the year.
"It is a delicate problem, a thorny problem, that has a very political dimension," he said.
